newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS-Fidelity sees more stability in fund heads.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Fidelity sees more stability in fund heads.

text.p: After a year-and-a-half of heavy portfolio manager turnover, the head of Fidelity Investments' mutual funds expects a return to more stability.

"I feel pretty confident that we won't have the sort of turnover in manager ranks that we did last year," Robert Pozen, who took over Fidelity's mutual fund division in late April, told reporters on Wednesday.

Twenty-three mutual fund managers have left the company since the beginning of last year, many opting for the higher pay and freedom at hedge funds. The exodus caused confusion among fund holders and industry analysts to question whether the best talent was walking out the door.

The most notable exit last year was Jeffrey Vinik, who managed the massive Magellan Fund, who left to form his own hedge fund after posting poor performance numbers over the last year of his tenure due to an ill-timed bet on bonds.

But a new compensation system put into place earlier this year should help stem the tide, Pozen said. Recent improved performance at many of Fidelity's diversified domestic stock funds will also help, he said.
"We're having more fun," he said. "Obviously improved numbers helps. People who were unhappy and dissatisfied, those people have left."

Pozen said he expected to change managers at one of Fidelity's Select funds, which focus on a particular market sector, and another fund manager will be stepping down over the next year. However, the turmoil among the ranks of fund managers should end, he said.

The departure of many fund managers and poor performance at a number of mutual funds spurred Fidelity to switch managers of 24 funds in March, 1996, and at another seven funds in June last year, and at 12 funds in January.

Pozen said that among the 31 funds which got new managers last year, 69 percent have outperformed at least half of their peers since the change. In the 12 months before the change, only 21 percent of the 31 funds placed among the top 50 percent of their peer group.
"The bulk of the manager changes from last year have been quite successful," he said. "The one-year numbers were off last year, and now we're starting to turn that around."
"Despite the sort of negative publicity that Magellan's performance generated a few years ago, the performance story here has turned around," he said.

Still, analysts said that many of Fidelity's diversified domestic stock funds are still posting disappointing returns, especially some of the larger funds with veteran managers such as the $27.6 billion Fidelity Contrafund.
"There's just not a lot there yet to point to that's really encouraging," said John Bonnanzio, editor of the independent publication Fidelity Insight.
